conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Dr. Harper, a clinician who specializes in mood and anxiety concerns that can come up after a baby is born. To help me understand how things have been feeling for you lately, I’d like to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale. It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been coping and feeling over the past week. Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team, and this is a judgment-free space—no right or wrong answers. We’ll go one question at a time at your pace.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not as much as I used to. I still chuckle when my older niece sends me those silly cat videos, but it feels muted—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or distracted by the baby’s breathing to really find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most of the time I can still laugh, but it’s definitely harder than it used to be. I’ll smile at a funny text or when my husband makes a joke, yet it feels kind of forced—like I’m not getting the full joy out of it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my mom bringing over dinner or taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but the excitement feels kind of dull. It’s more “that’ll be pleasant” than the bubbly, can’t-wait feeling I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy, or that I wasn’t soothing him right. I know babies just cry, but it’s hard not to feel like I must have done something wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I guess… yes. Most evenings, once my husband’s gone to bed, I sit in the nursery rocker and watch the baby breathe. I know he’s fine, but I still feel this tightness in my chest, waiting for something bad to happen. There isn’t any real reason—it’s just there.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing and I feel shaky, even though nothing’s wrong. Last night the baby stirred and I shot straight up in bed with this rush of fear, but he was just shifting in his sleep. It passed after a minute, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Between feedings every three hours, trying to shower, answering texts from well-meaning relatives, and the pile of laundry that never shrinks, I end up thinking, “I can’t keep up.” I’m not falling apart, but it’s exhausting trying to stay afloat.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do feel sad sometimes, but the sleep trouble feels more like my mind won’t shut off about the baby—checking the monitor, replaying whether I burped him long enough—than outright unhappiness keeping me awake. I’ll drift off fine, then wake around two or three and lie there an hour before I can settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’ve had moments. It’s not all day or every day, but sometimes—especially when the baby’s napping and the house is quiet—I’ll just feel this heaviness settle in. I’ll tear up a little, feel kind of empty, then it lifts after a while. So, yes, sad or miserable fits, but it comes and goes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like yesterday when I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded with one hand—but the tears never actually fell. I get that choked-up feeling, but I haven’t sat down and really cried all week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed or low, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

You've shared that the past week has felt like treading water-still able to smile at a text or look forward to a walk, yet the joy seems dulled and worry arrives uninvited each night. You blame yourself when your baby fusses, feel sudden waves of panic at small stirrings, and carry a persistent heaviness that lifts only briefly. Despite these challenges, you have stayed connected to loved ones and have not had thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports reduced enjoyment and a dulled excitement, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient admits blaming herself "some of the time" and gives specific examples of self-blame over normal infant crying</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic episodes ("a couple of times") with clear physical symptoms and sudden onset, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily struggle and exhaustion while still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient denies direct link to unhappiness but describes persistent middle-of-the-night wakefulness and intrusive, anxious thoughts about the baby, matching "Yes, sometimes" for sleep disruption related to low mood.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 16 places you well above the 13-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with likely comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. You describe core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>the excitement feels kind of dull</quote>), feelings of worthlessness/guilt (<quote>I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy</quote>), psychomotor agitation (<quote>my heart starts racing</quote>), sleep disruption, and recurrent worry without cause. Frequency and persistence exceed two weeks and impair daily functioning, yet you deny self-harm, placing you in the urgent-referral but non-emergent category. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> within the next 7 days to discuss formal diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request a referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>; ask whether an <med>SSRI compatible with breastfeeding</med> is appropriate
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS or <med>PHQ-9</med> in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
4. Implement low-pressure self-care: 20-minute stroller walks, brief shower while a trusted adult watches baby, and five-minute breathing breaks when the <sym>tightness</sym> rises
5. Share these results with a supportive partner, family member, or friend who can accompany you to appointments and help with night feedings so you can obtain 3-4 hour stretches of sleep
6. Bookmark 24/7 support lines (for example, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) for moments when worries intensify outside office hours
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [enter today]  Source: self-report  Weeks postpartum: [enter if known]

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (reduced enjoyment/pleasure) – Q1, Q2  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame – Q3  
- Persistent, unbidden worry (“waiting for something bad”) – Q4  
- Episodic panic symptoms (nocturnal surge, palpitations) – Q5  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to “keep up” – Q6  
- Intermittent low mood, emptiness, tearfulness – Q7, Q8, Q9  
- Initial and middle insomnia (monitor-checking, rumination) – Q7  

Symptoms denied  
- No crying spells of clinical intensity  
- No self-harm ideation – Q10  

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging since delivery; functional impact moderate (sleep disruption, daily tasks feel “exhausting”). No safety concerns at present.  

Screening significance  
Meets possible criteria for minor/major postpartum depression and comorbid postpartum anxiety; does not currently indicate high-risk safety status. Recommend routine follow-up with PCP/obstetric provider and formal depression/anxiety assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7) within 1–2 weeks; consider referral to perinatal mental health if symptoms persist or worsen.
